title: Swift Concurrency Part 3: @concurrent, Sendable & @unchecked Sendable
subtitle: This is Part 2 of a 3-part series on Swift Concurrency, Mainly focused on @concurrent, Sendable & @unchecked Sendable

body.title: Setting the Scene
body.text: By this point you understand actors, async/await, and Task. You can write safe concurrent code for most situations. Part 3 goes deeper into three topics that trip up even experienced Swift developers:

1. [tag]@concurrent:[/tag] explicitly running work off the current actor onto a background thread
2. [tag]Sendable:[/tag] the compiler's guarantee that values are safe to cross concurrency boundaries
3. [tag]@unchecked Sendable:[/tag] the escape hatch, and exactly when it's justified

body.title: The Problem It Solves
body.text:
In Part 1 we saw that actor methods run on the actor's executor. In Part 2 we saw that [tag]Task {}[/tag] inherits the actor context of the call site. In Swift 6.2 this extended to a third case: [tag]nonisolated async[/tag] functions also stay on the caller's actor by default.
Before Swift 6.2, calling any [tag]nonisolated async[/tag] function from a [tag]@MainActor[/tag] context silently hopped off the main thread to the global thread pool even when there was no reason to. This produced a constant stream of [tag]Sendable[/tag] errors and confusing debugging sessions.
Swift 6.2 fixes this: [tag]nonisolated async[/tag] functions stay on the caller's actor unless you explicitly say otherwise. And [tag]@concurrent[/tag] is how you say otherwise.

body.title: 1: A CPU-Bound Workload
body.text: To make [tag]@concurrent[/tag] tangible we need something that actually costs CPU time. This function burns cycles computing a sum, a stand-in for real work like JSON decoding, image processing, or cryptography:

Using real computation matters here. [tag]Task.sleep[/tag] (from Part 2) just suspends, it doesn't put load on any thread. To show that [tag]@concurrent[/tag] actually moves work off the main actor, we need a function that genuinely keeps a thread busy.
This actor wraps the CPU work and exposes two versions of the same function, one isolated (runs on the actor's serial executor) and one [tag]@concurrent[/tag] (hops to the global thread pool):
The signatures are identical. The only difference is [tag]@concurrent[/tag]. That single keyword changes where the body executes.

body.code:
let processor = WorkProcessor()
// Isolated: serialised. Total time ≈ A + B
print("=== Isolated (serialised) ===")
let startIsolated = Date()
async let a = processor.processIsolated(label: "A", iterations: 50_000_000)
async let b = processor.processIsolated(label: "B", iterations: 50_000_000)
_ = await (a, b)
let isolatedTotal = Date().timeIntervalSince(startIsolated) * 1000
print("  Total: \(String(format: "%.0f", isolatedTotal))ms\n")
// @concurrent: parallel. Total time ≈ max(A, B)
print("=== @concurrent (parallel) ===")
let startConcurrent = Date()
async let c = processor.processConcurrent(label: "C", iterations: 50_000_000)
async let d = processor.processConcurrent(label: "D", iterations: 50_000_000)
_ = await (c, d)
let concurrentTotal = Date().timeIntervalSince(startConcurrent) * 1000
print("  Total: \(String(format: "%.0f", concurrentTotal))ms")

body.text: Expected output:

body.code:
=== Isolated (serialised) ===
  [A] starting on actor executor...
  [A] done in 120ms
  [B] starting on actor executor...   ← B waits for A to finish
  [B] done in 118ms
  Total: 240ms
=== @concurrent (parallel) ===
  [C] starting on background thread...
  [D] starting on background thread...   ← D starts immediately, doesn't wait
  [C] done in 122ms
  [D] done in 119ms
  Total: 124ms   ← roughly half the time

body.text: The isolated version takes ~240ms. A finishes, then B starts. The [tag]@concurrent[/tag] version takes ~124ms. both run at the same time on separate threads.

body.title: When to Use `@concurrent`
body.text: Use it for CPU-bound work that genuinely benefits from parallelism:

rows: JSON / Protobuf decoding of large payloads

body.title: What Is `Sendable`?
body.text: [tag]Sendable[/tag] is a protocol with no methods or properties. It's purely a compiler-checked promise: "values of this type are safe to pass across concurrency boundaries."

When you send a value from one actor to another or capture it inside a [tag]Task[/tag] Swift verifies the type is [tag]Sendable[/tag]. If it isn't, you get a compile error. This is the compiler stopping a data race before it happens.

body.code:
// Sendable has no requirements: conformance is a promise, not an implementation
public protocol Sendable {}

body.title: 4: What Is Automatically `Sendable`?
body.text: Swift synthesises [tag]Sendable[/tag] conformance for types it can prove are safe. You rarely need to write it explicitly for structs and enums:

The rule for automatic synthesis:
  • [tag]struct[/tag] / [tag]enum[/tag]: synthesised if all stored properties / associated values are [tag]Sendable[/tag]
  • [tag]class[/tag]: synthesised only if all stored properties are [tag]let[/tag] and [tag]Sendable[/tag], and the class is [tag]final[/tag]

body.title: What It Is
body.text: [tag]@unchecked[/tag] Sendable tells the compiler: "Trust me: this type is safe across concurrency boundaries, but don't verify it."
The compiler stops checking. Thread safety is now entirely your responsibility.

body.title: 6: A Legitimate Use: Lock-Protected Cache
body.text: The most honest use of [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag] is wrapping a mutable class that protects itself with a lock. The compiler can't see through the lock to verify safety. you can, so you take responsibility:

Every access goes through [tag]lock.withLock {}[/tag]. The [tag]NSLock[/tag] genuinely serialises reads and writes, this is thread-safe. The compiler can't see that, so we tell it to trust us with [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag].

body.title: The Line You Must Not Cross

body.text:
Adding [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag] without actual synchronisation doesn't make the type safe. It just silences the compiler while leaving a data race in place. The runtime has no mercy for this.
Before reaching for [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag], check if a better alternative fits:

rows: Mutable state always on the main thread
Bridging a documented thread-safe ObjC type
Silencing a warning you don't understand

body.title: Summary
body.text: [tag]@concurrent[/tag]

list: New in Swift 6.2. Hops an async function off the current actor onto the global thread pool.
Without it, `nonisolated async functions` stay on the caller's actor (the new default in 6.2).
Use for CPU-bound work: decoding, image processing, cryptography, compression.
Don't use for network calls `URLSession` already suspends without blocking.

body.text: [tag]Sendable[/tag]

list: A compiler-checked promise that a value is safe to cross concurrency boundaries.
Synthesised automatically for structs/enums with `Sendable` properties, and for `final class` with all `let` properties.
The compiler enforces this at every actor boundary and Task capture, it's your first line of defence against data races.

body.text: [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag]

list: Silences the compiler's `Sendable` check. Thread safety is entirely your responsibility.
Justified for lock-protected mutable classes and documented thread-safe Objective-C types.
Never use it just to silence a warning you don't understand. A data race is worse than a compile error.

body.text:
• Read SE-0461: the proposal behind the Swift 6.2 [tag]nonisolated[/tag] default change.
  • Enable Thread Sanitizer ([tag]Product → Scheme → Run → Diagnostics[/tag]) during development. It catches data races at runtime that the compiler can miss, especially around [tag]@unchecked Sendable[/tag].
  • Look into [tag]withCheckedContinuation[/tag] and [tag]withCheckedThrowingContinuation[/tag] for wrapping legacy callback-based APIs into clean async functions.
